### Working draft (~175 words) — Option A

> Read through the RAT lens already applied in this study (Hughes et al., 2006), the group contrast reported above is analytically useful: it situates each app relative to prior classroom activity rather than scoring teachers as persons. That framing alone, however, does not settle how the contrast should be interpreted professionally. Accounts of technology integration that treat pedagogical knowledge developed in practice as central to sophisticated redesign would lead one to expect in-service teachers to display at least comparable—and often greater—capacity for innovative technology use than pre-service teachers (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Under that expectation, a group difference in which more ambitious redesign appears less concentrated among in-service designs is not merely a descriptive asymmetry. It is a point of theoretical friction: the observation, as framed by RAT, sits in partial tension with an experience-based understanding of innovative capacity. The task of this discussion is therefore not to restate which group coded “higher,” but to interpret a pattern that RAT makes visible yet that practice-centered innovation expectations leave under-explained.

### Friction structure (explicit)

| | Role |
|---|------|
| **Theory 1** | RAT (Hughes et al., 2006) — frames the already-reported contrast |
| **Theory 2** | Practice-centered pedagogical knowledge / TPACK (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) — predicts IST ≥ PST innovative capacity |
| **Conflict** | Framed observation sits in partial tension with that prediction |

### Theory 2 options

| | Theory 2 | If you prefer… |
|---|----------|----------------|
| **A** *(default above)* | Mishra & Koehler (2006) TPACK | Clean, one cite each |
| **B** | Sherin & van Es (2009) / Goodwin (1994) noticing | Experience should *see* richer redesign |
| **C** | Zhao et al. (2002) classroom innovation conditions | Softer, fit-centered prediction |

The findings of this study suggest that pre-service teachers' designs tend to align more closely with the amplification level of the RAT framework, while in-service teachers' designs cluster toward replacement. This pattern, when viewed through the lens of RAT, raises interesting questions about the role of pedagogical expertise in technology integration.
